blocks.text: Compression molding is a manufacturing process that uses heat and pressure to form rubber, silicone, or thermoset plastic materials into custom components.

During the process, a measured amount of material, often called a preform or charge, is placed directly into a heated mold cavity. The mold is then closed under pressure, causing the material to flow and conform to the desired geometry.
Heat and pressure initiate the curing process, transforming the material into a finished component with its intended physical and mechanical properties.
Once curing is complete, the mold opens, and the finished part is removed for any required trimming, inspection, or secondary operations.
Compression molding is widely used to manufacture industrial components requiring specialized materials, robust construction, and reliable performance.

items.title: Material Versatility
body: A broad selection of rubber, silicone, and rigid thermoset materials can be compression molded to meet application-specific requirements.

items.title: Engineered Material Performance
body: Compression molding supports components designed for abrasion resistance, chemical exposure, temperature extremes, vibration isolation, and mechanical durability.

items.title: Production Flexibility
body: The process can accommodate prototype programs, specialized lower-volume components, and ongoing production requirements.

items.title: Bonded Assemblies
body: Compression molding can be used to produce rubber-to-metal and other bonded components that combine multiple materials into a finished assembly.

sections.heading: Compression Molding vs. Transfer Molding vs. Injection Molding

blocks.text: Selecting the right molding process depends on component geometry, material requirements, production volume, and tooling economics.

items.title: Compression Molding
body: Often well suited for large components, thick cross sections, relatively straightforward geometries, and specialized rubber or thermoset materials.

items.title: Transfer Molding
body: Can provide advantages for complex geometries, molded-in inserts, bonded assemblies, and applications requiring controlled material flow into closed mold cavities.

items.title: Injection Molding
body: May offer advantages for complex components and repeat production, particularly when part volumes and cycle-time requirements justify the tooling and equipment investment.
SYNC offers multiple molding processes, allowing our engineering teams to evaluate the most appropriate manufacturing solution rather than relying on a single process.

items.q: What is compression molding used for?
a: Compression molding is commonly used to manufacture rubber, silicone, and thermoset plastic components such as seals, gaskets, vibration isolators, valve components, bushings, industrial pads, and bonded assemblies.

items.q: Is compression molding suitable for large rubber parts?
a: Yes. Compression molding is particularly well suited for many large-format and thick-section rubber components. The maximum part dimensions depend on the available press capacity, mold configuration, and material requirements.

items.q: What is the difference between compression molding and transfer molding?
a: Compression molding places material directly into the mold cavity before applying heat and pressure. Transfer molding forces material from a separate chamber into a closed mold cavity.
Transfer molding can be advantageous for complex shapes and inserts, while compression molding may provide tooling and processing advantages for larger or simpler components.

items.q: Can different rubber materials be compression molded?
a: Yes. Common materials include natural rubber, EPDM, nitrile, silicone, neoprene, SBR, and specialty elastomers.

items.q: Can compression molding be used for rubber-to-metal bonded parts?
a: Yes. With suitable substrate preparation, bonding chemistry, material selection, and tooling, rubber can be bonded to metal during compression molding.

items.q: Does SYNC support prototype and production quantities?
a: Yes. SYNC supports prototype development, specialized low-volume applications, and recurring production programs. The most appropriate manufacturing process depends on the component and program requirements.

items.q: Can SYNC help determine the right rubber compound?
a: Yes. Our material and engineering teams can evaluate hardness, chemical exposure, operating temperature, mechanical requirements, and other performance specifications to help identify suitable elastomer formulations.
